summary.one_liner: Vim is a long-established, highly extensible text editor that is an improved version of the classic UNIX vi editor, used for editing programs and plain text.
summary.what_it_does: Vim extends the original vi editor with multi-level undo, syntax highlighting, command-line history, on-line help, spell checking, filename completion, block operations, and a script language. It keeps Vi compatibility while adding a graphical user interface option. Commands are typed with normal keyboard characters, function keys can be remapped to commands, and the mouse can be used. A minimal build (vim.tiny) aims to provide a mostly POSIX-compatible vi, and many Linux distributions use it as the default vi. The README says Vim runs on MS-Windows, macOS, Haiku, VMS and most UNIX flavours. Documentation is built in via :help, with a one-hour tutor (vimtutor) and a user manual.
use_cases: editing source code in a terminal
replacing vi on a Linux system
customizing an editor with scripts and key mappings
how_to_run: Install Vim through your system's package manager (the README notes it is often available there)
Run vimtutor for a one-hour beginner course
Inside Vim, run :help to open the built-in documentation
For source builds, see src/INSTALL and README_unix.txt or the platform-specific README files
notable: Vi-compatible with many added features such as multi-level undo and syntax highlighting
Built-in help system and a user manual
Runs on MS-Windows, macOS, Haiku, VMS and most UNIX variants
vim.tiny minimal build used as default vi on many Linux distributions
caveats: Older versions for MS-DOS, Windows 95/98/Me/NT/2000/XP/Vista, Amiga DOS, BeOS, RISC OS and OS/2 are no longer maintained
Source builds require compiling from the src directory per src/INSTALL
Vi compatibility means a modal, keyboard-driven learning curve
summary.license: Vim license (Charityware); the README says it is GPL compatible. Summary: unmodified copies may be used and distributed freely, and modified versions have a few restrictions.
